Amgen CEO Bob Bradway's 2025 Letter to Shareholders | Amgen
Amgen CEO Bob Bradway's 2025 Letter to Shareholders | Amgen

content.text:
**Overall:** Amgen’s main strength is its scale: it has a broad commercial portfolio that is still growing despite pressure on some older blockbuster drugs. Its main weaknesses are patent-driven sales erosion, pricing and reimbursement pressure, and the uncertainty inherent in replacing established drugs with newer products and pipeline candidates.

### Strengths
- **Large, diversified portfolio and strong cash generation.** In 2025, Amgen reported $36.8 billion in revenue, $8.1 billion in free cash flow, and 14 products with annual sales above $1 billion. In Q2 2026, revenue rose 10% year over year to $10.1 billion; 22 products had double-digit sales growth. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/stories/2026/03/2025-letter-to-shareholders))
- **Several meaningful growth products.** Repatha and Evenity grew strongly in 2025, as did oncology and rare-disease medicines such as Blincyto and Tezspire. In Q2 2026, Repatha sales grew 37% and Evenity 38%. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Substantial R&D and development potential.** Amgen invested $7.3 billion in R&D in 2025. Its pipeline includes MariTide, a potential obesity treatment now in Phase 3 trials; if successful, it could open a large market, though that outcome is far from certain. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/stories/2026/03/2025-letter-to-shareholders))
- **Strong operating capabilities.** Amgen has global commercial reach and major biologics-manufacturing capacity, with further U.S. manufacturing investments planned. Those capabilities can support the development and launch of complex medicines. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/stories/2026/03/2025-letter-to-shareholders))

### Weaknesses and risks
- **Biosimilar competition is already cutting into important products.** Patents covering Prolia and Xgeva expired in the U.S. in February 2025. In Q2 2026, Prolia sales fell 32% and Xgeva fell 34% year over year, with Amgen citing biosimilar competition. Enbrel is also under pressure: its 2025 sales fell 33%. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Pricing and reimbursement can offset volume growth.** Amgen identifies government and private-payer cost controls as risks. CMS-set Medicare Part D prices for Enbrel took effect in 2026, and Otezla’s are scheduled for 2027; Amgen expects those prices to hurt profitability in Medicare. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Pipeline success isn’t guaranteed.** New drugs and expanded indications must clear clinical trials and regulatory review. A promising program such as MariTide could be delayed, fail, or prove less commercially successful than hoped. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Meaningful debt and manufacturing concentration.** At June 30, 2026, Amgen reported $57.3 billion in debt and $14.0 billion in cash. It also says most commercial manufacturing is at its Puerto Rico facility, leaving supply exposed to a major disruption there. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000124/amgn-20260630earningsrelea.htm))

**Bottom line:** Amgen is a large, cash-generative company with multiple growing products—not a one-drug story. But investors and business observers should watch whether growth products and pipeline launches can compensate for the ongoing decline of older, heavily exposed medicines, while also accounting for pricing pressure and debt.
